That upon the whole matter we are <hi type="italic">God's offspring;</hi> he is <hi type="italic">our Father that begat us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.6">Deut. xxxii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.18">18</reference>), and he hath <hi type="italic">nourished and brought us up as children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Isa. i. 2</reference>. The confession of an adversary in such a case is always looked upon to be of use as <hi type="italic">argumentum ad hominem—an argument to the man,</hi> and therefore the apostle here quotes a saying of one of the Greek poets, Aratus, a native of Cilicia, Paul's countryman, who, in his <hi type="italic">Phenomena,</hi> in the beginning of his book, speaking of the heathen <hi type="italic">Jupiter,</hi> that is, in the poetical dialect, the supreme <hi type="italic">God,</hi> says this of him, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tou gar kai genos esmen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">for we are also his offspring.</hi> And he might have quoted other poets to the purpose of what he was speaking, that <hi type="italic">in God we live and move:</hi>— <div eID="gen29816" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen29817"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29818"/>Spiritus intus alit, totamque infusa per artus<l eID="gen29818" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29819"/>Mens agitat molem.<l eID="gen29819" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29820"/>This active mind, infus'd through all the space,<l eID="gen29820" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29821"/>Unites and mingles with the mighty mass.—<hi type="italic">Virgil,</hi> Æneid vi.<l eID="gen29821" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29822"/>Est Deus in nobis, agitante calescimus illo.<l eID="gen29822" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29823"/>'Tis the Divinity that warms our hearts.—<hi type="italic">Ovid,</hi> Fast. vi.<l eID="gen29823" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29824"/>Jupiter est quodeunque vides,<l eID="gen29824" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29825"/>Quocunque moveris.<l eID="gen29825" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29826"/>Where'er you look, where'er you rove<l eID="gen29826" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen29827"/>The spacious scene is full of Jove.—<hi type="italic">Lucan,</hi> lib. ii.<l eID="gen29827" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen29817"/> <div sID="gen29828" type="x-p"/> III. From all these great truths concerning God, he infers the absurdity of their idolatry, as the prophets of old had done. If this be so, 1. Then God cannot be represented by an image. If we are <hi type="italic">the offspring of God,</hi> as we are spirits in flesh, then certainly he who is <hi type="italic">the Father of our spirits</hi> (and they are the principal part of us, and that part of us by which we are denominated God's offspring) is himself a Spirit, and we ought not to think that the Godhead is <hi type="italic">like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.17.29">v. 29</reference>. We wrong God, and put an affront upon him, if we think so. God honoured man in making his soul after his own likeness; but man dishonours God if he makes him after the likeness of his body. The Godhead is spiritual, infinite, immaterial, incomprehensible, and therefore it is a very false and unjust conception which an image gives us of God, be the matter ever so rich, <hi type="italic">fold or silver;</hi> be the shape ever so curious, and be it ever so well <hi type="italic">graven by art or man's device,</hi> its countenance, posture, or dress, ever so significant, it is a teacher of lies. 2. Then <hi type="italic">he dwells not in temples made with hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.17.24">v. 24</reference>. He is not invited to any temple men can build for him, nor confined to any. A temple brings him never the nearer to us, nor keeps him ever the longer among us. A temple is convenient for us to come together in to worship God; but God needs not any place of rest or residence, nor the magnificence and splendour of any structure, to add to the glory of his appearance. A pious, upright heart, <hi type="italic">a temple not made with hands,</hi> but by <hi type="italic">the Spirit of God,</hi> is that which <hi type="italic">he dwells in,</hi> and <hi type="italic">delights to dwell in.</hi> See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.27">1 Kings viii. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1-Isa.66.2">Isa. lxvi. 1, 2</reference>. 3. Then he is <hi type="italic">not worshipped,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">therapeuetai</hi></hi>, he is <hi type="italic">not served,</hi> or <hi type="italic">ministered unto, with men's hands, as though he needed any thing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.17.25">v. 25</reference>. He that made all, and maintains all, cannot be benefited by any of our services, nor needs them. If we receive and derive all from him, he is all-sufficient, and therefore cannot but be self-sufficient, and independent. What need can God have of our services, or what benefit can he have by them, when he has all perfection in himself, and we have nothing that is good but what we have from him? The philosophers, indeed, were sensible of this truth, that God has no need of us or our services; but the vulgar heathen built temples and offered sacrifices to their gods, with an opinion that they needed houses and food. See <reference osisRef="Job.35.5-Job.35.8">Job xxxv. 5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Ps. l. 8</reference>, &c. 4. Then it concerns us all to enquire after God (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">That they should seek the Lord,</hi> that is, fear and worship him in a right manner. Therefore God has kept the children of men in a constant dependence upon him for life and all the comforts of life, that he might keep them under constant obligations to him. We have plain indications of God's presence among us, his presidency over us, the care of his providence concerning us, and his bounty to us, that we might be put upon enquiring, <hi type="italic">Where is God our Maker, who giveth songs in the night, who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wiser than the fowls of heaven?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.35.10-Job.35.11">Job xxxv. 10, 11</reference>. Nothing, one would think, should be more powerful with us to convince us that there is a God, and to engage us to seek his honour and glory in our services, and to seek our happiness in his favour and love, than the consideration of our own nature, especially the noble powers and faculties of our own souls. If we reflect upon these, and contemplate these, we may perceive both our relation and obligation to a God above us. Yet so dark is this discovery, in comparison with that by divine revelation, and so unapt are we to receive it, that those who have no other could but <hi type="italic">haply feel after God</hi> and <hi type="italic">find him.</hi> (1.) It was very uncertain whether they could by this searching <hi type="italic">find out God;</hi> it is but a peradventure: <hi type="italic">if haply</hi> they might. (2.) If they did find out something of God, yet it was but some confused notions of him; they did but feel after him, as men in the dark, or blind men, who lay hold on a thing that comes in their way, but know not whether it be that which they are in quest of or no. It is a very confused notion which this poet of theirs has of the relation between God and man, and very general, that <hi type="italic">we are his offspring:</hi> as was also that of their philosophers. Pythagoras said, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Theion genos esti brotoios</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Men have a sort of a divine nature.</hi> And Heraclitus (<hi type="italic">apud Lucian</hi>) being asked, <hi type="italic">What are men?</hi> answered, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Theoi thnetoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Mortal gods;</hi> and, <hi type="italic">What are the gods?</hi> answered, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">athanatoi anthropoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Immortal men.</hi> And Pindar saith (<hi type="italic">Nemean, Ode</hi> 6), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">En andron hen theon genos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">God and man are near a-kin.</hi> It is true that by the knowledge of ourselves we may be led to the knowledge of God, but it is a very confused knowledge. This is but feeling after him. We have therefore reason to be thankful that by the gospel of Christ we have notices given us of God much clearer than we could have by the light of nature; we do not now feel after him, but <hi type="italic">with open face behold, as in a glass, the glory of God.</hi> <div eID="gen29828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29829" type="x-p"/> IV. He proceeds to call them all to repent of their idolatries, and to turn from them, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.30-Acts.17.31">v. 30, 31</reference>. This is the practical part of Paul's sermon before the university; having declared God to them (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.23">v. 23</reference>), he properly presses upon them <hi type="italic">repentance towards God,</hi> and would also have taught them <hi type="italic">faith towards our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> if they had had the patience to hear him. Having shown them the absurdity of their worshipping other gods, he persuades them to go on no longer in that foolish way of worship, but to return from it to the living and true God. Observe, <div eID="gen29829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29830" type="x-p"/> 1. The conduct of God towards the Gentile world before the gospel came among them: <hi type="italic">The times of this ignorance God winked at.</hi> (1.) They were times of great ignorance. Human learning flourished more than ever in the Gentile world just before Christ's time; but in the things of God they were grossly ignorant. Those are ignorant indeed who either know not God or worship him ignorantly; idolatry was owing to ignorance. (2.) These times of ignorance God winked at. Understand it, [1.] As an act of divine justice. God despised or neglected these times of ignorance, and did not send them his gospel, as now he does. It was very provoking to him to see his glory thus given to another; and he detested and hated these times. So some take it. Or rather, [2.] As an act of divine patience and forbearance. He winked at these times; he did not restrain them from these idolatries by sending prophets to them, as he did to Israel; he did not punish them in their idolatries, as he did Israel; but gave them the gifts of his providence, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.16-Acts.14.17">ch. xiv. 16, 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">These things thou hast done, and I kept silence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.21">Ps. l. 21</reference>. He did not give them such calls and motives to repentance as he does now. He <hi type="italic">let them alone.</hi> Because they did not improve the light they had, but were willingly ignorant, he did not send them greater lights. Or, he was not quick and severe with them, but was long-suffering towards them, because they did it ignorantly, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13">1 Tim. i. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen29830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29831" type="x-p"/> 2. The charge God gave to the Gentile world by the gospel, which he now sent among them: <hi type="italic">He now commandeth all men every where to repent</hi>—to change their mind and their way, to be ashamed of their folly and to act more wisely, to break off the worship of idols and bind themselves to the worship of the true God. Nay, it is to turn with sorrow and shame from every sin, and with cheerfulness and resolution to every duty. (1.) This is God's command. It had been a great favour if he had only told us that there was room left for repentance, and we might be admitted to it; but he goes further, he interposes his own authority for our good, and has made that our duty which is our privilege. (2.) It is his command to <hi type="italic">all men, every where,</hi>—to men, and not to angels, that need it not,—to men, and not to devils, that are excluded the benefit of it,—to all men in all places; all men have made work for repentance, and have cause enough to repent, and all men are invited to repent, and shall have the benefit of it. The apostles are commissioned to preach this every where. The prophets were sent to command the Jews to repent; but the apostles were sent to preach <hi type="italic">repentance and remission of sins to all nations.</hi> (3.) Now in gospel times it is more earnestly commanded, because more encouraged than it had been formerly. Now the way of remission is more opened than it had been, and the promise more fully confirmed; and therefore now he expects we should all repent. "Now repent; now at length, now in time, repent; for you have too long gone on in sin. Now in time repent, for it will be too late shortly." <div eID="gen29831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29832" type="x-p"/> 3. The great reason to enforce this command, taken from the judgment to come. God commands us to repent, <hi type="italic">because he hath appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.31">v. 31</reference>), and has now under the gospel made a clearer discovery of a state of retribution in the other world than ever before. Observe, (1.) The God that made the world will judge it; he that gave the children of men their being and faculties will call them to an account for the use they have made of them, and recompense them accordingly, whether the body served the soul in serving God or the soul was a drudge to the body in making provision for the flesh; and <hi type="italic">every man shall receive according to the things done in the body,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">2 Cor. v. 10</reference>. The God that now governs the world will judge it, will reward the faithful friends of his government and punish the rebels. (2.) There is a day appointed for this general review of all that men have done in time, and a final determination of their state for eternity. The day is fixed in the counsel of God, and cannot be altered; but it is his there, and cannot be known. A day of decision, a day of recompence, a day that will put a final period to all the days of time. (3.) The world will be judged in righteousness; for God is not unrighteous, who taketh vengeance; far be it from him that he should do iniquity. His knowledge of all men's characters and actions is infallibly true, and therefore his sentence upon them incontestably just. And, as there will be no appeal from it, so there will be no exception against it. (4.) God will judge the world <hi type="italic">by that man whom he hath ordained,</hi> who can be no other than the Lord Jesus, to whom all judgment is committed. By him God made the world, by him he redeemed it, by him he governs it, and by him he will judge it. (5.) God's raising Christ from the dead is the great proof of his being appointed and ordained the Judge of quick and dead. His doing him that honour evidenced his designing him this honour. His raising him from the dead was the beginning of his exaltation, his judging the world will be the perfection of it; and he that begins will make an end. God hath <hi type="italic">given assurance unto all men,</hi> sufficient ground for their faith to build upon, both that there is a judgment to come and that Christ will be their judge; the matter is not left doubtful, but is of unquestionable certainty. Let all his enemies be assured of it, and tremble before him; let all his friends be assured of it, and triumph in him. (6.) The consideration of the judgment to come, and of the great hand Christ will have in that judgment, should engage us all to repent of our sins and turn from them to God. This is the only way to make the Judge our friend in that day, which will be a terrible day to all who live and die impenitent; but true penitents will then <hi type="italic">lift up their heads with joy, knowing that their redemption draws nigh.</hi>
entries.bf7340192effaed2fd98635d19181c6583edc395: <div eID="gen29832" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul at Athens.</title> <div sID="gen29833" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this <hi type="italic">matter.</hi> <hi type="super">33</hi> So Paul departed from among them. 34 Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which <hi type="italic">was</hi> Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them. <div eID="gen29833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29834" type="x-p"/> We have here a short account of the issue of Paul's preaching at Athens. <div eID="gen29834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29835" type="x-p"/> I. Few were the better: the gospel had as little success at Athens as any where; for the pride of the philosophers there, as of the Pharisees at Jerusalem, prejudiced them against the gospel of Christ. 1. Some ridiculed Paul and his preaching. They heard him patiently till he came to speak of the resurrection of the dead (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.32">v. 32</reference>), and then some of them began to hiss him: they <hi type="italic">mocked.</hi> What he had said before was somewhat like what they had sometimes heard in their own schools, and some notion they had of a resurrection, as it signifies a future state; but, if he speak of a <hi type="italic">resurrection of the dead,</hi> though it be of the resurrection of Christ himself, it is altogether incredible to them, and they cannot bear so much as to hear of it, as being contrary to a principle of their philosophy: <hi type="italic">A privatione ad habitum non datur regressus—Life when once lost is irrecoverable.</hi> They had deified their heroes after their death, but never thought of their being raised from the dead, and therefore they could by no means reconcile themselves to this doctrine of Christ's being raised from the dead; how can this be? This great doctrine, which is the saints' joy, is their jest; when it was but mentioned to them they mocked, and made a laughing matter of it. We are not to think it strange if sacred truths of the greatest certainty and importance are made the scorn of profane wits. 2. Others were willing to take time to consider of it; they said, <hi type="italic">We will hear thee again of this matter.</hi> They would not at present comply with what Paul said, nor oppose it; but <hi type="italic">we will hear thee again of this matter,</hi> of the resurrection of the dead. It should seem, they overlooked what was plain and uncontroverted, and shifted off the application and the improvement of that, by starting objections against what was disputable, and would admit a debate. Thus many lose the benefit of the practical doctrine of Christianity, by wading beyond their depth into controversy, or, rather, by objecting against that which has some difficulty in it; whereas, if any man were disposed and determined to <hi type="italic">do the will of God,</hi> as far as it is discovered to him, he should <hi type="italic">know of the doctrine of Christ,</hi> that it is <hi type="italic">of God, and not of man,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. Those that would not yield to the present convictions of the word thought to get clear of them, as Felix did, by putting them off to another opportunity; they will hear of it again some time or other, but they know not when; and thus the devil cozens them of all their time, by cozening them of the present time. 3. Paul thereupon left them for the present to consider of it (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">He departed from amongst them,</hi> as seeing little likelihood of doing any good with them at this time; but, it is likely, with a promise to those that were willing to hear him again that he would meet them whenever they pleased. <div eID="gen29835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29836" type="x-p"/> II. Yet there were some that were wrought upon, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.34">v. 34</reference>. If some would not, others would. 1. There were certain men that adhered to him, and believed. When he departed from amongst them, they would not part with him so; wherever he went, they would follow him, with a resolution to adhere to the doctrine he preached, which they believed. 2. Two are particularly named; one was an eminent man, <hi type="italic">Dionysius the Areopagite,</hi> one of that high court or great council that sat in Areopagus, or Mars' Hill—a judge, a senator, one of those before whom Paul was summoned to appear; his judge becomes his convert. The account which the ancients give of this Dionysius is that he was bred at Athens, had studied astrology in Egypt, where he took notice of the miraculous eclipse at our Saviour's passion,—that, returning to Athens, he became a senator, disputed with Paul, and was by him converted from his error and idolatry; and, being by him thoroughly instructed, was made the first bishop of Athens. So <hi type="italic">Eusebius, lib.</hi> 5, <hi type="italic">cap.</hi> 4; <hi type="italic">lib.</hi> 4, <hi type="italic">cap.</hi> 22. The <hi type="italic">woman named Damaris</hi> was, as some think, the wife of Dionysius; but, rather, some other person of quality; and, though there was not so great a harvest gathered in at Athens as there was at other places, yet, these few being wrought upon there, Paul had no reason to say he had <hi type="italic">laboured in vain.</hi>  <chapter eID="Acts.17"/> <div eID="gen29836" type="x-p"/>

entries.f326b6486e23e6ef9985b8de46e37786dc8c95de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15997"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 17</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.17.1-Acts.17.15">Ac 17:1-15</reference>. At Thessalonica the Success of Paul's Preaching Endangering His Life, He Is Despatched by Night to Berea, Where His Message Meets with Enlightened Acceptance--A Hostile Movement from Thessalonica Occasions His Sudden Departure from Berea--He Arrives at Athens.</title> <div sID="gen30867" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15997"/><hi type="bold">1. when they had passed through Amphipolis--</hi>thirty-three miles southwest of Philippi, on the river Strymon, and at the head of the gulf of that name, on the northern coast of the Ægean Sea.<div eID="gen30867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30868" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Apollonia--</hi>about thirty miles southwest of Amphipolis; but the exact site is not known.<div eID="gen30868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30869" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they came to Thessalonica--</hi>about thirty-seven miles due west from Apollonia, at the head of the Thermaic (or Thessalonian) Gulf, at the northwestern extremity of the Ægean Sea; the principal and most populous city in Macedonia. "We see at once how appropriate a place it was for one of the starting-points of the Gospel in Europe, and can appreciate the force of what Paul said to the Thessalonians within a few months of his departure from them: "From you, the word of the Lord sounded forth like a trumpet, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place,"" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.8">1Th 1:8</reference>) [Howson].<div eID="gen30869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">where was a synagogue of the Jews--</hi>implying that (as at Philippi) there was none at Amphipolis and Apollonia. <div eID="gen30870" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3d8832d6f1eabab345d51065078966f8248aba9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15998"/><div sID="gen30871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15998"/><hi type="bold">2-4. Paul, as his manner was--</hi>always to begin with the Jews.<div eID="gen30871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went in unto them--</hi>In writing to the converts but a few months after this, he reminds them of the courage and superiority to indignity, for the Gospel's sake, which this required after the shameful treatment he had so lately experienced at Philippi (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">1Th 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen30872" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b094fe984b569ce7ff6c03661f89db83f7d4cf1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16001"/><div sID="gen30877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16001"/><hi type="bold">5-9. the Jews ... moved with envy--</hi>seeing their influence undermined by this stranger.<div eID="gen30877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lewd fellows of the baser sort--</hi>better, perhaps, "worthless market people," that is, idle loungers about the market-place, of indifferent character.<div eID="gen30878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gathered a company--</hi>rather, "having raised a mob."<div eID="gen30879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">assaulted the house of Jason--</hi>with whom Paul and Silas abode (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.7">Ac 17:7</reference>), one of Paul's kinsmen, apparently (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.21">Ro 16:21</reference>), and from his name, which was sometimes used as a Greek form of the word Joshua [Grotius], probably a Hellenistic Jew.<div eID="gen30880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30881" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sought to bring them--</hi>Jason's lodgers. <div eID="gen30881" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7506b373864f2ee4d022ac4ebfe79b5b2cc1990: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16005"/><div sID="gen30887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16005"/><hi type="bold">10-12. the brethren immediately sent away Paul and Silas by night--</hi>for it would have been as useless as rash to attempt any further preaching at that time, and the conviction of this probably made his friends the more willing to pledge themselves against any present continuance of missionary effort.<div eID="gen30887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto Berea--</hi>fifty or sixty miles southwest of Thessalonica; a town even still of considerable population and importance. <div eID="gen30888" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8bb02591b0b47d6871ece73e6cd3a2131948b58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16008"/><div sID="gen30895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16008"/><hi type="bold">13. the Jews of Thessalonica ... came thither also--</hi>"like hunters upon their prey, as they had done before from Iconium to Lystra" [Howson]. <div eID="gen30895" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f64552fb7599f73df23412ccf002df2fb2d8cbb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16009"/><div sID="gen30896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16009"/><hi type="bold">14. immediately the brethren--</hi>the converts gathered at Berea.<div eID="gen30896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent away Paul--</hi>as before from Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.30">Ac 9:30</reference>), and from Thessalonica (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.10">Ac 17:10</reference>). How long he stayed at Berea we know not; but as we know that he longed and expected soon to return to the Thessalonians (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.17">1Th 2:17</reference>), it is probable he remained some weeks at least, and only abandoned his intention of revisiting Thessalonica at that time when the virulence of his enemies there, stimulated by his success at Berea, brought them down thither to counterwork him.<div eID="gen30897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to go as it were to the sea--</hi>rather, perhaps, "in the direction of the sea." Probably he delayed fixing his next destination till he should reach the coast, and the providence of God should guide him to a vessel bound for the destined spot. Accordingly, it was only on arriving at Athens, that the convoy of Berean brethren, who had gone thus far with him, were sent back to bid Silas and Timothy follow him thither.<div eID="gen30898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Silas and Timotheus abode there still--</hi>"to build it up in its holy faith, to be a comfort and support in its trials and persecutions, and to give it such organization as might be necessary" [Howson]. Connecting this with the apostle's leaving Timothy and Luke at Philippi on his own departure (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.16.40">Ac 16:40</reference>), we may conclude that this was his fixed plan for cherishing the first beginning of the Gospel in European localities, and organizing the converts. Timotheus must have soon followed the apostle to Thessalonica, the bearer, probably, of one of the Philippian "contributions to his necessity" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.15">Php 4:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">16</reference>), and from thence he would with Silas accompany him to Berea. <div eID="gen30899" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7696cbc0d5ce9becbac4674108fc1d32cb1a58c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16010"/><div sID="gen30900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16010"/><hi type="bold">15. Silas and Timotheus to come to him with all speed--</hi>He probably wished their company and aid in addressing himself to so new and great a sphere as Athens. Accordingly it is added that he "waited for them" there, as if unwilling to do anything till they came. That they did come, there is no good reason to doubt (as some excellent critics do). For though Paul himself says to the Thessalonians that he "thought it good to be left at Athens alone" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.1">1Th 3:1</reference>), he immediately adds that he "sent Timotheus to establish and comfort them" (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.2">Ac 17:2</reference>); meaning, surely, that he despatched him from Athens back to Thessalonica. He had indeed sent for him to Athens; but, probably, when it appeared that little fruit was to be reaped there, while Thessalonica was in too interesting a state to be left uncherished, he seems to have thought it better to send him back again. (The other explanations which have been suggested seem less satisfactory). Timotheus rejoined the apostle at Corinth (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">Ac 18:5</reference>). <div eID="gen30900" type="x-p"/>
entries.c8b2f7b95649db47548912204c81b66f2628685e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16011"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.17.16-Acts.17.34">Ac 17:16-34</reference>. Paul at Athens.</title> <div sID="gen30901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16011"/><hi type="bold">16-17. wholly given to idolatry--</hi>"covered with idols"; meaning the city, not the inhabitants. Petronius, a contemporary writer at Nero's court, says satirically that it was easier to find a god at Athens than a man. This "stirred the spirit" of the apostle. "The first impression which the masterpieces of man's taste for art left on the mind of St. Paul was a revolting one, since all this majesty and beauty had placed itself between man and his Creator, and bound him the faster to his gods, who were not God. Upon the first contact, therefore, which the Spirit of Christ came into with the sublimest creations of human art, the judgment of the Holy Ghost--through which they have all to pass--is set up as "the strait gate," and this must remain the correct standard for ever" [Baumgarten]. <div eID="gen30901" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a57612b7c51eba935ecc0ce165c4ecdac653d4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16013"/><div sID="gen30907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16013"/><hi type="bold">18-21. certain ... of the Epicureans--</hi>a well-known school of atheistic materialists, who taught that pleasure was the chief end of human existence; a principle which the more rational interpreted in a refined sense, while the sensual explained it in its coarser meaning.<div eID="gen30907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and of the Stoics--</hi>a celebrated school of severe and lofty pantheists, whose principle was that the universe was under the law of an iron necessity, the spirit of which was what is called the Deity: and that a passionless conformity of the human will to this law, unmoved by all external circumstances and changes, is the perfection of virtue. While therefore the Stoical was in itself superior to the Epicurean system, both were alike hostile to the Gospel. "The two enemies it has ever had to contend with are the two ruling principles of the Epicureans and Stoics--Pleasure and Pride" [Howson].<div eID="gen30908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">What will this babbler say?--</hi>The word, which means "a picker-up of seeds," bird-like, is applied to a gatherer and retailer of scraps of knowledge, a prater; a general term of contempt for any pretended teacher.<div eID="gen30909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a setter forth of strange gods--</hi>"demons," but in the Greek (not Jewish) sense of "objects of worship."<div eID="gen30910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because he preached Jesus and the resurrection--</hi>Not as if they thought he made these to be two divinities: the strange gods were Jehovah and the Risen Saviour, ordained to judge the world. <div eID="gen30911" type="x-p"/>
entries.9996cb28bfe36c157a74b624b1697edffc1a252f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16016"/><div sID="gen30914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16016"/><hi type="bold">22. Then Paul stood ... and said--</hi>more graphically, "standing in the midst of Mars' hill, said." This prefatory allusion to the position he occupied shows the writer's wish to bring the situation vividly before us [Baumgarten].<div eID="gen30914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious--</hi>rather (with most modern interpreters and the ancient Greek ones), "in all respects extremely reverential" or "much given to religious worship," a conciliatory and commendatory introduction, founded on his own observation of the symbols of devotion with which their city was covered, and from which all Greek writers, as well as the apostle, inferred the exemplary religiousness of the Athenians. (The authorized translation would imply that only too much superstition was wrong, and represents the apostle as repelling his hearers in the very first sentence; whereas the whole discourse is studiously courteous). <div eID="gen30915" type="x-p"/>
entries.c150d0abeecc149f9d128301ae3d5df3033acccb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16017"/><div sID="gen30916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16017"/><hi type="bold">23. as I passed by and beheld your devotions--</hi>rather, "the objects of your devotion," referring, as is plain from the next words, to their works of art consecrated to religion.<div eID="gen30916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I found an altar ... To the--</hi>or, "an"<div eID="gen30917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30918" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unknown god--</hi>erected, probably, to commemorate some divine interposition, which they were unable to ascribe to any known deity. That there were such altars, Greek writers attest; and on this the apostle skilfully fastens at the outset, as the text of his discourse, taking it as evidence of that dimness of religious conception which, in virtue of his better light, he was prepared to dissipate.<div eID="gen30918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship--</hi>rather, "Whom, therefore, knowing Him not, ye worship," alluding to "The Unknown God."<div eID="gen30919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him declare--</hi>announce.<div eID="gen30920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I unto you--</hi>This is like none of his previous discourses, save that to the idolaters of Lycaonia (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.15-Acts.14.17">Ac 14:15-17</reference>). His subject is not, as in the synagogues, the Messiahship of Jesus, but THE Living God, in opposition to the materialistic and pantheistic polytheism of Greece, which subverted all true religion. Nor does he come with speculation on this profound subject--of which they had had enough from others--but an authoritative "announcement" of Him after whom they were groping not giving Him any name, however, nor even naming the Saviour Himself but unfolding the true character of both as they were able to receive it. <div eID="gen30921" type="x-p"/>
entries.79289d970963f39b36fad7a15ab10374b27242c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16018"/><div sID="gen30922" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16018"/><hi type="bold">24-25. God that made the world and all ... therein--</hi>The most profound philosophers of Greece were unable to conceive any real distinction between God and the universe. Thick darkness, therefore, behooved to rest on all their religious conceptions. To dissipate this, the apostle sets out with a sharp statement of the fact of creation as the central principle of all true religion--not less needed now, against the transcendental idealism of our day.<div eID="gen30922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seeing he is Lord--</hi>or Sovereign.<div eID="gen30923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of heaven and earth--</hi>holding in free and absolute subjection all the works of His hands; presiding in august royalty over them, as well as pervading them all as the principle of their being. How different this from the blind Force or Fate to which all creatures were regarded as in bondage!<div eID="gen30924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelleth not in temples made with hands--</hi>This thought, so familiar to Jewish ears (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.27">1Ki 8:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1">Is 66:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.48">Ac 7:48</reference>), and so elementary to Christians, would serve only more sharply to define to his heathen audience the spirituality of that living, personal God, whom he "announced" to them. <div eID="gen30925" type="x-p"/>
entries.44cd88521d8ac02257bafd033628a64d0680690c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16020"/><div sID="gen30930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16020"/><hi type="bold">26-27. and hath made of one blood all nations of men to dwell on all the face of the earth--</hi>Holding with the Old Testament teaching, that in the blood is the life (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Ge 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.17.11">Le 17:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.23">De 12:23</reference>), the apostle sees this life stream of the whole human race to be one, flowing from one source [Baumgarten].<div eID="gen30930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation--</hi>The apostle here opposes both Stoical Fate and Epicurean Chance, ascribing the periods and localities in which men and nations flourish to the sovereign will and prearrangements of a living God. <div eID="gen30931" type="x-p"/>
entries.eeedc03fc632c62cafe6ae00f8f07aeb303bf2f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16022"/><div sID="gen30936" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16022"/><hi type="bold">28. For in him we live, and move, and have our being--</hi>(or, more briefly, "exist").--This means, not merely, "Without Him we have no life, nor that motion which every inanimate nature displays, nor even existence itself" [Meyer], but that God is the living, immanent Principle of all these in men.<div eID="gen30936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring--</hi>the first half of the fifth line, word for word, of an astronomical poem of Aratus, a Greek countryman of the apostle, and his predecessor by about three centuries. But, as he hints, the same sentiment is to be found in other Greek poets. They meant it doubtless in a pantheistic sense; but the truth which it expresses the apostle turns to his own purpose--to teach a pure, personal, spiritual Theism. (Probably during his quiet retreat at Tarsus. <reference osisRef="Acts.9.30">Ac 9:30</reference>, revolving his special vocation to the Gentiles he gave himself to the study of so much Greek literature as might be turned to Christian account in his future work. Hence this and his other quotations from the Greek poets, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.33">1Co 15:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.12">Tit 1:12</reference>). <div eID="gen30937" type="x-p"/>
entries.480c623d47e5a84c3d7c13fa1c171cdb6ac0f8ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16023"/><div sID="gen30938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16023"/><hi type="bold">29. Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think--</hi>The courtesy of this language is worthy of notice.<div eID="gen30938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device--</hi>("graven by the art or device of man"). One can hardly doubt that the apostle would here point to those matchless monuments of the plastic art, in gold and silver and costliest stone, which lay so profusely beneath and around him. The more intelligent pagan Greeks no more pretended that these sculptured gods and goddesses were real deities, or even their actual likenesses, than Romanist Christians do their images; and Paul doubtless knew this; yet here we find him condemning all such efforts visibly to represent the invisible God. How shamefully inexcusable then are the Greek and Roman churches in paganizing the worship of the Christian Church by the encouragement of pictures and images in religious service! (In the eighth century, the second council of Nicea decreed that the image of God was as proper an object of worship as God Himself). <div eID="gen30939" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3d82738e48b07cf38575a824f1f273e5492b630: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16024"/><div sID="gen30940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16024"/><hi type="bold">30. the times of this ignorance God winked at--</hi>literally (and far better), "overlooked," that is, bore with, without interposing to punish it, otherwise than suffering the debasing tendency of such worship to develop itself (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.14.16">Ac 14:16</reference>, and see on <reference osisRef="Rom.1.24">Ro 1:24</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen30940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but now--</hi>that a new light was risen upon the world.<div eID="gen30941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commandeth--</hi>"That duty--all along lying upon man estranged from his Creator, but hitherto only silently recommending itself and little felt--is now peremptory."<div eID="gen30942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30943" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all men every where to repent--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.6">Col 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.11">Tit 1:11</reference>)--a tacit allusion to the narrow precincts of favored Judaism, within which immediate and entire repentance was ever urged. The word "repentance" is here used (as in <reference osisRef="Luke.13.3">Lu 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.10">15:10</reference>) in its most comprehensive sense of "repentance unto life." <div eID="gen30943" type="x-p"/>
entries.be3a453c36baf3602bf66bd6a0f00ff8c23f9a1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16025"/><div sID="gen30944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16025"/><hi type="bold">31. Because he hath appointed a day in the which he will judge the world--</hi>Such language beyond doubt teaches that the judgment will, in its essence, be a solemn judicial assize held upon all mankind at once. "Aptly is this uttered on the Areopagus, the seat of judgment" [Bengel].<div eID="gen30944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30945" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by that man whom he hath ordained--</hi>compare <reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, 23, 27; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.42">Ac 10:42</reference>.<div eID="gen30945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead--</hi>the most patent evidence to mankind at large of the judicial authority with which the Risen One is clothed. <div eID="gen30946" type="x-p"/>
entries.267486859630e79863b584ecaaeb74f3ee8caa34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16026"/><div sID="gen30947" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16026"/><hi type="bold">32-34. when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked--</hi>As the Greek religion was but the glorification of the present life, by the worship of all its most beauteous forms, the Resurrection, which presupposes the vanity of the present life, and is nothing but life out of the death of all that sin has blighted, could have no charm for the true Greek. It gave the death blow to his fundamental and most cherished ideas; nor until these were seen to be false and fatal could the Resurrection, and the Gospel of which it was a primary doctrine, seem otherwise than ridiculous.<div eID="gen30947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">others said, We will hear thee again of this--</hi>"an idle compliment to Paul and an opiate to their consciences, such as we often meet with in our own day. They probably, like Felix, feared to hear more, lest they should be constrained to believe unwelcome truths" (<reference osisRef="Acts.24.25">Ac 24:25</reference>; and compare <reference osisRef="Matt.13.15">Mt 13:15</reference>) [Webster and Wilkinson]. <div eID="gen30948" type="x-p"/>

entries.a5dc441e2efff3288e0de2d28ec9c34a0a174ad5: <div eID="gen44818" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen44819" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen44820" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen44820" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen44819" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen44821" type="x-p"/> Paul and his company, passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, come to Thessalonica, were they preach the Gospel to the Jews, several of whom believe, <reference osisRef="Act.17.1-Act.17.4">Act 17:1-4</reference>. Others raise a mob, and bring Jason, who had received the apostles, before the magistrates, who, having taken bail of him and his companions, dismiss them, <reference osisRef="Act.17.5-Act.17.9">Act 17:5-9</reference>. Paul and Silas are sent away by night unto Berea, where they preach to the Jews, who gladly receive the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Act.17.10-Act.17.12">Act 17:10-12</reference>. Certain Jews from Thessalonica, hearing that the Bereans had received the Gospel, come thither and raise up a persecution, <reference osisRef="Act.17.13">Act 17:13</reference>. Paul is sent away by the brethren to Athens, where he preaches to the Jews, <reference osisRef="Act.17.14-Act.17.17">Act 17:14-17</reference>. He is encountered by the Epicureans and Stoics, who bring him to the Areopagus, and desire him to give a full explanation of his doctrine, <reference osisRef="Act.17.18-Act.17.20">Act 17:18-20</reference>. The character of the Athenians, <reference osisRef="Act.17.21">Act 17:21</reference>. Paul preaches to them, and gives a general view of the essential principles of theology, <reference osisRef="Act.17.22-Act.17.31">Act 17:22-31</reference>. Some mock, some hesitate, and some believe, and, among the latter, Dionysias and Damaris, <reference osisRef="Act.17.32-Act.17.34">Act 17:32-34</reference>. <div eID="gen44821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44822" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen44822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44823" type="x-p"/> Passed through Amphipolis - This city was the metropolis of the first division of Macedonia, as made by Paulus Aemilius: see the note on <reference osisRef="Act.16.10">Act 16:10</reference>. It was builded by Cimon, the Athenian general, who sent 10,000 Athenians thither as a colony. It stood in an island in the river Strymon, and had its name of Amphipolis because included between the two grand branches of that river where they empty themselves into the sea, the river being on both sides of the city. <div eID="gen44823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44824" type="x-p"/> Apollonia - This was another city of Macedonia, between Amphipolis and Thessalonica. It does not appear that St. Paul stopped at any of these cities: and they are only mentioned by the historian as places through which the apostles passed on their way to Thessalonica. It is very likely that in these cities there were no Jews; and that might have been the reason why the apostles did not preach the Gospel there, for we find them almost constantly beginning with the Jews; and the Hellenist Jews, living among the Gentiles, became the medium through which the Gospel of Christ was conveyed to the heathen world. <div eID="gen44824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44825" type="x-p"/> Thessalonica - This was a celebrated city of Macedonia, situated on what was called the Thermaic Gulf. According to Stephanus Byzantinus, it was embellished and enlarged by Philip, king of Macedon, who called it Thessalonica, the victory of Thessalia, on account of the victory he obtained there over the Thessalians; but, prior to this, it was called Thermae. But Strabo, Tzetzes, and Zonaras, say that it was called Thessalonica, from Thessalonica, wife of Cassander, and daughter of Philip. It is now in possession of the Turks, and is called Salonichi, which is a mere corruption of the original name. <div eID="gen44825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44826" type="x-p"/> A synagogue of the Jews - Ἡ συναγωγη, The synagogue; for the article here must be considered as emphatic, there probably being no other synagogue in any other city in Macedonia. The Jews in different parts had other places of worship called proseuchas. as we have seen, <reference osisRef="Act.16.13">Act 16:13</reference>. At Thessalonica alone they appear to have had a synagogue.
entries.5fdd7fad9b2bc4f0016fbff37b90efb1806d9894: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen44826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44827" type="x-p"/> As his manner was - He constantly offered salvation first to the Jews; and for this purpose attended their Sabbath-days' meetings at their synagogues.
entries.7943f5477748701dfd1364c027e7e9953e08e226: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen44827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44828" type="x-p"/> Opening and alleging - Παρατιθεμνος, Proving by citations. His method seems to have been this: 1st. He collected the scriptures that spoke of the Messiah. 2d. He applied these to Jesus Christ, showing that in him all these scriptures were fulfilled, and that he was the Savior of whom they were in expectation. He showed also that the Christ, or Messiah, must needs suffer - that this was predicted, and was an essential mark of the true Messiah. By proving this point, he corrected their false notion of a triumphant Messiah, and thus removed the scandal of the cross.
entries.11da502b219b9a1257e75200902865ce98e686e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen44828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44829" type="x-p"/> The devout Greeks - That is, Gentiles who were proselytes to the Jewish religion, so far as to renounce idolatry, and live a moral life, but probably had not received circumcision.
entries.2f1ed96687a761a9a60423d9eff25bb411651345: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen44829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44830" type="x-p"/> The Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them - Instead of this sentence, the most correct MSS. and versions read simply, προσλαβομενοι δε οἱ Ιουδαιοι. But the Jews taking, etc., leaving out the words, ζηλωσαντες, απειθουντες, which believed not, moved with envy: these words do not appear to be genuine; there is the strongest evidence against them, and they should be omitted. <div eID="gen44830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44831" type="x-p"/> Certain lewd fellows of the baser sort - This is not a very intelligible translation. The original is, των αγοραιων τινας ανδοας πονηρους. The word αγοραιοι, which we translate the baser sort, is by Hesychius explained, οἱ εν αγορᾳ αναϚρεφομενοι, those who transact business in courts of justice. The same word is used by the Jews in Hebrew letters to signify judges; and אגוריאות של גוים agorioth shel goyim, signifies judges of the Gentiles. These were probably a low kind of lawyers, what we would call pettifoggers, or attorneys without principle, who gave advice for a trifle, and fomented disputes and litigations among the people. The Itala version of the Codex Bezae calls them quosdam forenses, certain lawyers. As the Jews, from their small number, could not easily raise up a mob, they cunningly employed those unprincipled men, who probably had a certain degree of juridical credit and authority, to denounce the apostles as seditious men; and this was, very likely, the reason why they employed those in preference to any others. They were such as always attended forensic litigations, waiting for a job, and willing to defend any side of a question for money. They were wicked men of the forensic tribe. <div eID="gen44831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44832" type="x-p"/> Gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar - And, after having made this sedition and disturbance, charged the whole on the peaceable and innocent apostles! This is precisely the same way that persecution against the truth and followers of Christ is still carried on. Some wicked man in the parish gets a wicked attorney and a constable to head a mob, which they themselves have raised; and, having committed a number of outrages, abusing men and women, haul the minister of Christ to some magistrate who knows as little of his office as he cares for the Gospel; they there charge the outrages which themselves have committed on the preacher and his peaceable hearers; and the peacemaker, appointed by a good king, according to the wise and excellent regulations of a sound constitution, forgetting whose minister he is, neither administers justice nor maintains truth; but, espousing the part of the mob, assumes, ex officio, the character of a persecutor. The preacher is imprisoned, his hearers fined for listening to that Gospel which has not only made them wise unto salvation, but also peaceable and orderly citizens, and which would have had the same effect on the unprincipled magistrate, the parish squire, and the mob, had they heard it with the same reverence and respect. Had I not witnessed such scenes, and such prostitution of justice, I could not have described them. <div eID="gen44832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44833" type="x-p"/> Assaulted the house of Jason - This was the place where the apostles lodged; and therefore his goods were clear spoil, and his person fair game. This is a case which frequently occurs where the Gospel is preached in its spirit and power. And, even in this moat favored kingdom, the most scandalous excesses of this kind have been committed, and a justice of the peace has been found to sanction the proceedings; and, when an appeal has been made to the laws, a grand jury has been found capable of throwing out the true bill!
entries.f154103ef068b30772890bef0619b552dc174613: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen44833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44834" type="x-p"/> These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also - The very character our forefathers had for preaching that Gospel, in every part of the land, by which the nation has been illuminated, the mob disciplined into regularity and order, and the kingdom established in the hands of the best of monarchs.
entries.37f304b7d3957ff553c3bc6077a75582a4177403: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen44834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44835" type="x-p"/> These all do contrary to the decrees of Caesar - Persecutors always strive to affect the lives of the objects of their hatred, by accusing them of sedition, or plots against the state. <div eID="gen44835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44836" type="x-p"/> That there is another king, one Jesus - How malevolent was this saying! The apostles proclaimed Jesus as king - that is true; but never once insinuated that his kingdom was of this world. The reverse they always maintained.
entries.560ae742a881509878f14997cab9a53e3b9f2d2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen44836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44837" type="x-p"/> And they troubled the people and the rulers - It is evident that there was no disposition in either the people or the rulers to persecute the apostles. But these wicked Jews, by means of the unprincipled, wicked lawyers, those lewd fellows of the baser sort, threw the subject into the form of law, making it a state question, in which form the rulers were obliged to notice it; but they showed their unwillingness to proceed in a matter which they saw proceeded from malice, by letting Jason and his companions go off on bail.
entries.394987d159933ee62c2f7150c4b52a700dc80b14: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen44837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44838" type="x-p"/> Taken security - Λαβοντες το ἱκανον, Having taken what was sufficient, or satisfactory. Sufficient for the present, to prove that the apostles were upright, peaceable, and loyal men; and that Jason and his friends were the like, and would be, at any time, forthcoming to answer for their conduct. Perhaps this is the sense of the phrase in the text.
entries.9adfee960799a7d553cb41032788fb837674c9e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen44838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44839" type="x-p"/> Sent away Paul and Silas by night - Fearing some farther machinations of the Jews and their associates. <div eID="gen44839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44840" type="x-p"/> Berea - This was another city of Macedonia, on the same gulf with Thessalonica; and not far from Pella, the birth place of Alexander the Great.
entries.066d0fda283d364c5dad44ebf424e42bc5ab819a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen44840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44841" type="x-p"/> These were more noble than those in Thessalonica - Ησαν ευγενεϚεροι, Were of a better race, extraction, or birth, than those at Thessalonica; but the word refers more to their conduct, as a proof of their better disposition, than to their birth, or any peculiar lineal nobility. It was a maxim among the Jews, that "none was of a noble spirit who did not employ himself in the study of the law." It appears that the Bereans were a better educated and more polished people than those at Thessalonica; in consequence far from persecuting: <div eID="gen44841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44842" type="x-p"/> 1. They heard the doctrine of the Gospel attentively. <div eID="gen44842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44843" type="x-p"/> 2. They received this doctrine with readiness of mind: when the evidence of its truth appeared to them sufficiently convincing, they had too much dignity of mind to refuse their assent, and too much ingenuousness to conceal their approbation. <div eID="gen44843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44844" type="x-p"/> 3. They searched the Scriptures, i.e. of the Old Testament, to see whether these thing were so: to see whether the promises and types corresponded with the alleged fulfillment in the person, works, and sufferings of Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen44844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44845" type="x-p"/> 4. They continued in this work; they searched the Scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
entries.d2040b817875ad5e25d1ef57e116a45463bb4d76: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen44845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44846" type="x-p"/> Therefore many of them believed - From the manner in which they heard, received, and examined the word preached to them, it was not likely they could be deceived. And, as it was the truth that was proclaimed to them, it is no wonder that they apprehended, believed, and embraced it. <div eID="gen44846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44847" type="x-p"/> Of honorable women which were Greeks - Probably mere heathens are meant; and these were some of the chief families in the place. Thus we find that the preaching of Paul at Berea was made the instrument of converting both Jews and Gentiles.
entries.3d0c4df64bdf6fd09d9ed59545dd8dca97959672: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen44847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44848" type="x-p"/> The Jews of Thessalonica - stirred up the people - With what implacable malice did these men persecute the Gospel! And in the same spirit they continue to the present day, though it is evidently the sole cause of their wretchedness.
entries.1bb962585b42d23df53a78946af8f0f43f454f6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen44848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44849" type="x-p"/> To go as it were to the sea - This passage is generally understood to mean that the disciples took Paul towards the sea, as if he had intended to embark, and return to Troas, but with the real design to go to Athens. But it is more likely that his conductors, in order to his greater safety, left the public or more frequented road, and took him coastwise to Athens. Or, by taking a vessel at that part of the sea nearest to Berea, they might have coasted it to Athens, which was quite a possible case; and, as we do not hear of his stopping at any place on his journey to preach, it is very probable that he went by sea to this city. Though sleights and feints may be allowable in cases of life and death, yet there does not appear an absolute necessity for any in this case. And, as the text does not necessarily point any out, so we need not have recourse to any. I take it for granted, therefore, that Paul went by sea to Athens. <div eID="gen44849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44850" type="x-p"/> Silas and Timotheus abode there still - The persecution, it seems, was directed principally against Paul. Lo! he stayeth his rough wind on the day of his east wind. Silas and Timotheus, holy men, were left behind to water the seed which Paul had planted.
entries.8766ba5151a6e32f8de0d3e4d8e70ff33b9e198d: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen44850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44851" type="x-p"/> Brought him unto Athens - This was one of the most celebrated cities in the world, whether we consider its antiquity, its learning, its political consequence, or the valor of its inhabitants. This city, which was the capital of Attica, and the seat of the Grecian empire was founded by Cecrops, about a.m. 2447, before Christ 1557, and was called by him Cecropia. About thirteen or fourteen hundred years before Christ, in the reign either of Erechtheus, or Erichthonius, it was called Athens, from Αθηνη, a name of Minerva, to whom it was dedicated, and who was always considered the protectress of the city. The whole city at first was built upon a hill or rock, in the midst of a spacious plain; but, in process of time, the whole plain was covered with buildings which were called the lower city; while the ancient was called Acropolis, or the upper city. In its most flourishing state this city was not less than one hundred and seventy-eight stadia, or twenty-two Roman miles in circumference. The buildings of Athens were the most superb, and best executed, in the world; but every thing is now in a state of ruin. Mr. Stuart, in his three folio vols. of the Antiquities of Athens, has given correct representations of those that remain, with many geographical notices of much importance. The greatest men that ever lived, scholars, lawyers, statesmen, and warriors, were Athenians. Its institutions, laws, and literature, were its own unrivalled boast, and the envy of the world. The city still exists; the Acropolis in a state of comparative repair. It is now in the hands of the Greeks; but the Turks, who held it till lately, have turned the celebrated Parthenon, or temple of Minerva, into a mosque. The inhabitants are reckoned at about one thousand. Christianity, planted here by St. Paul, still subsists; and about two-thirds of the inhabitants of Athens are Christians, who have several churches or oratories here, and it is the residence of a Greek bishop, who is a metropolitan. He who considers the ancient glory of this city, whether in its heathen or Christian antiquity, cannot but sigh over its present state.
entries.017344b70265f5e26efcc4832fedd3a4b8cde8a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen44851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44852" type="x-p"/> He saw the city wholly given to idolatry - Κατειδωλον, Full of idols, as the margin has it, and very properly. Whoever examines the remains of this city, as represented by Mr. Stuart in his Antiquities, already referred to, will be satisfied of the truth of St. Luke's remark: it was full of idols. Bishop Pearce produces a most apposite quotation from Pausanias, which confirms the observation: Ουκ ην αλλαχου τοσαυτα ιδειν ειδωλα. There was no place where so many idols were to be seen. Paus. in Attic. cap. xvii. 24. <div eID="gen44852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44853" type="x-p"/> Petronius, who was contemporary with St. Paul, in his Satyr. cap. xvii., makes Quartilla say of Athens: Utique nostra regio tam Praesentibus Plena Est Numinibus, ut facilius possis Deum quam Hominem invenire. Our region is so full of deities that you may more frequently meet with a god than a man.
entries.bcd6ac4b36d1403ab4fa7dced788262ce4f0a21e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen44853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44854" type="x-p"/> Disputed he in the synagogue with the Jews - Proving that Jesus was the Messiah: and with the devout persons, probably heathens, proselyted to the Jewish religion. And in the market: I suppose the αγορα here means some such place as our exchange, where people of business usually met, and where the philosophers conversed and reasoned. The agora was probably like the Roman forum, and like places of public resort in all countries, where people of leisure assembled to converse, hear the news, etc.
entries.bfc97776b67966164839d0d340c27588d42c2c2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen44854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44855" type="x-p"/> Certain philosophers of the Epicureans - These were the followers of Epicurus, who acknowledged no gods except in name, and absolutely denied that they exercised any government over the world or its inhabitants; and that the chief good consisted in the gratification of the appetites of sense. These points the Epicureans certainly held; but it is not clear that Epicurus himself maintained such doctrines. <div eID="gen44855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44856" type="x-p"/> And of the Stoics - These did not deny the existence of the gods; but they held that all human affairs were governed by fate. They did not believe that any good was received from the hands of their gods; and considered, as Seneca asserts, that any good and wise man was equal to Jupiter himself. Both these sects agreed in denying the resurrection of the body; and the former did not believe in the immortality of the soul. <div eID="gen44856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44857" type="x-p"/> Epicurus, the founder of the Epicurean sect, was born at Athens, about a.m. 3663, before Christ 341. <div eID="gen44857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44858" type="x-p"/> Zeno, the founder of the Stoic sect, was born in the isle of Cyprus, about thirty years before Christ. His disciples were called Stoics from the Στοα, a famous portico at Athens, where they studied. Besides these two sects, there were two others which were famous at this time; viz. the Academics and the Peripatetics. The founder of the first was the celebrated Plato; and the founder of the second, the no less famous Aristotle. These sects professed a much purer doctrine than the Epicureans and Stoics; and it does not appear that they opposed the apostles, nor did they enter into public disputations with them. Against the doctrines taught by the Epicureans and Stoics, several parts of St. Paul's discourse, in the following verses, are directly pointed. <div eID="gen44858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44859" type="x-p"/> What will this babbler say? - The word σπερμολογος, which we translate babbler, signifies, literally, a collector of seeds, and is the "name of a small bird the lives by picking up seeds on the road." The epithet became applied to persons who collected the sayings of others, without order or method, and detailed them among their companions in the same way. The application of the term to prating, empty, impertinent persons, was natural and easy, and hence it was considered a term of reproach and contempt, and was sometimes used to signify the vilest sort of men. <div eID="gen44859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44860" type="x-p"/> A setter forth of strange gods - Ξενων δαιμονιων, Of strange or foreign demons. That this was strictly forbidden, both at Rome and Athens, see on <reference osisRef="Act.16.21">Act 16:21</reference> (note). <div eID="gen44860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44861" type="x-p"/> There was a difference, in the heathen theology, between θεος, god, and δαιμων, demon: the θεοι, were such as were gods by nature: the δαιμονια, were men who were deified. This distinction seems to be in the mind of these philosophers when they said that the apostles seemed to be setters forth of strange demons, because they preached unto them Jesus, whom they showed to be a man, suffering and dying, but afterwards raised to the throne of God. This would appear to them tantamount with the deification of heroes, etc., who had been thus honored for their especial services to mankind. Horace expresses this in two lines, 2 Epist. i. 5: - <div eID="gen44861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44862" type="x-p"/> Romulus, et Liber pater, et cum Castore Pollux, <div eID="gen44862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44863" type="x-p"/> Post ingentia facta, deorum in templa recepti. "Romulus, father Bacchus, with Castor and Pollux, for their eminent services, have been received into the temples of the gods."
entries.a5512ee03c601df2f64ac74a6d3ba5fdb6acccf1: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen44863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44864" type="x-p"/> They took him, and brought him unto Areopagus - The Areopagus was a hill not far from the Acropolis, already described, where the supreme court of justice was held; one of the most sacred and reputable courts that had ever existed in the Gentile world. It had its name, Αρειος παγος, Areopagus, or the Hill of Mars, or Ares, from the circumstance, according to poetic fiction, of Mars being tried there, by a court of twelve gods, for the murder of Halirrhothius, son of Neptune: the meaning of which is, that Ares, a Thessalian prince, having slain Halirrhothius, the son of a neighboring prince, for having violated his daughter Alcippe, was here tried by twelve judges, by whom he was honourably acquitted: in the Athenian laws the death of the ravisher was the regular forfeiture for his crime. The justice administered in this court was so strict and impartial, that, it was generally allowed, both the plaintiff and defendant departed satisfied with the decision. "Innocence, when summoned before it, appeared without apprehension; and the guilty, convicted and condemned, retired without daring to murmur." The place in which the judges sat was uncovered; and they held their sittings by night, to the end that nothing might distract their minds from the great business on which they were to decide; and that the sight of the accused might not affect them either with pity or aversion. In reference to this, all pleaders were strictly forbidden to use any means whatever to excite either pity or aversion, or to affect the passions; every thing being confined to simple relation, or statement of facts. When the two parties were produced before the court, they were placed between the bleeding members of victims slain on the occasion, and were obliged to take an oath, accompanied by horrible imprecations on themselves and families, that they would testify nothing but truth. These parties called to witness the eumenides, or furies, the punishers of the perjured in the infernal world; and, to make the greater impression on the mind of the party swearing, the temple dedicated to these infernal deities was contiguous to the court, so that they appeared as if witnessing the oaths and recording the appeal made to themselves. When the case was fully heard, the judges gave their decision by throwing down their flint pebbles, on two boards or tables, one of which was for the condemnation, the other for the acquittal, of the person in question.
entries.66c3f88c7404cdc5b56f680ef130b32a15e6cd5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen44864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44865" type="x-p"/> Thou bringest - strange things to our ears - The doctrine of the apostles was different from any they had ever heard: it was wholly spiritual and divine; thus it was strange: it was contrary to their customs and manners; and thus it was strange also. As it spoke much of the exaltation and glory of Jesus Christ, they supposed him to be a setter forth of strange gods: and, therefore, on the authority of the laws, which forbade the introduction of any new deities, or modes of worship, he was called before the Areopagus.
entries.826295eec43a6dbf91a7e68075cdf30560ed4e13: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen44865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44866" type="x-p"/> All the Athenians and strangers which were there - As Athens was renowned for its wisdom and learning, it became a place of public resort for philosophers and students from different parts of the then civilized world. The flux of students was in consequence great; and these, having much leisure time, would necessarily be curious to know what was passing in the world, and would frequently assemble together, in places of public resort, to meet with strangers just come to the city; and either, as St. Luke says, to tell or hear some new thing. "The Athenian writers give the same account of their fellow citizens. Demosthenes, in his reply to Epist. Philippi, represents the Athenians as πυνθανομενοι κατα την αγοραν, ει τι λεγεται νεωτερον; inquiring, in the place of public resort, if there are any News. We find, likewise, that when Thucydides, iii. 38, had said, μετα καινοτητος μεν λογου απατασθαι αριϚοι, Ye are excellent in suffering yourselves to be deceived by Novelty of speech, the old scholiast makes this remark upon it, (almost in the words of St. Luke), ταυτα προς τους. Αθηναιους αινιττεται, ουδεν τι μελετωντας, πλην λεγειν τι και ακουειν καινον; He here blames the Athenians, who made it their only business to tell and hear something that was New." - Bp. Pearce. This is a striking feature of the city of London in the present day. The itch for news, which generally argues a worldly, shallow, or unsettled mind, is wonderfully prevalent: even ministers of the Gospel, negligent of their sacred function, are become in this sense Athenians; so that the book of God is neither read nor studied with half the avidity and spirit as a newspaper. These persons, forgetful not only of their calling, but of the very spirit of the Gospel, read the account of a battle with the most violent emotions; and, provided the victory falls to their favourite side, they exult and triumph in proportion to the number of thousands that have been slain! It is no wonder if such become political preachers, and their sermons be no better than husks for swine. To such the hungry sheep look up, and are not fed. God pity such miserable Athenians, and direct them to a more suitable employment!
entries.b39ae2c266fc9815e80a757916e0ac905d09921f: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen44866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44867" type="x-p"/> Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill - That is, in the midst of the judges, who sat in the Areopagus. <div eID="gen44867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44868" type="x-p"/> Ye are too superstitious - Κατα παντα ὡς δεισιδαιμονεϚερους ὑμας θεωρω; I perceive that in all respects ye are greatly addicted to religious practices; and, as a religious people, you will candidly hear what I have got to say in behalf of that worship which I practice and recommend. See farther observations at the end of the chapter.
entries.9686b5142d35703d37a7af625f508a54c055ebcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen44868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44869" type="x-p"/> Beheld your devotions - Σεβασματα, The objects of your worship; the different images of their gods which they held in religious veneration, sacrificial instruments, altars, etc., etc. <div eID="gen44869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44870" type="x-p"/> To the Unknown God - ΑΓΝΩΣΤΩ ΘΕΩ. That there was an altar at Athens thus inscribed, we cannot doubt after such a testimony; though St. Jerome questions it in part; for he says St. Paul found the inscription in the plural number, but, because he would not appear to acknowledge a plurality of gods, he quoted it in the singular: Verum, quia Paulus non pluribus Diis indigebat ignotis, sed uno tantum ignoto Deo, singulari verbo usus est. Epist. ad Magn. This is a most foolish saying: had Paul done so, how much would such a begging of the question have prejudiced his defense in the minds of his intelligent judges! Oecumenius intimates that St. Paul does not give the whole of the inscription which this famous altar bore; and which he says was the following: Θεοις Ασιας και Ευρωπης και Λιβυης, Θεῳ αγνωϚῳ και ξενῳ, To the gods of Asia, and Europe, and Africa: To The Unknown and strange God. Several eminent men suppose that this unknown god was the God of the Jews; and, as his name יהוה was considered by the Jews as ineffable, the Θεος αγνωϚος may be considered as the anonymous god; the god whose name was not known, and must not be pronounced. That there was such a god acknowledged at Athens we have full proof. Lucian in his Philopatris, cap. xiii. p. 769, uses this form of an oath: νη τον αγνωϚον τον εν Αθηναις, I swear by the Unknown God at Athens. And again, cap. xxix. 180: ἡμεις δε τον εν Αθηναις αγνωϚον εφευροντες και προσκυνησαντες, χειρας εις ουρανον εκτειναντες, τουτῳ ευχαριϚησομεν ὡς καταξιωθεντες, etc. We have found out the Unknown god at Athens - and worshipped him with our hands stretched up to heaven; and we will gave thanks unto him, as being thought worthy to be subject to this power. Bp. Pearce properly asks, Is it likely that Lucian, speaking thus, (whether in jest or in earnest), should not have had some notion of there being at Athens an altar inscribed to the unknown God? Philostratus, in vit. Apollon. vi. 3, notices the same thing, though he appears to refer to several altars thus inscribed: και ταυτα Αθηνῃσι, οὑ και αγνωϚων Θεων βωμοι ἱδρυνται, And this at Athens, where there are Altars even to the Unknown Gods. Pausanias, in Attic. cap. 1. p. 4, edit. Kuhn., says that at Athens there are βωμοι Θεων των ονομαζομενων αγνωϚων, altars of gods which are called, The Unknown ones.
